newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns against replay of "Great Game".
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns against replay of "Great Game".

text.p: A top U.S. policy-maker on Russia called on Monday for efforts to avoid a repeat of the 19th century "Great Game" in Central Asia in which major powers would compete for the region's vast oil and gas reserves.
Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott urged instead that conflict resolution should be "Job One" for U.S. policy in the turbulent region.

Tablbott said that since the Central Asian states shook off Soviet rule in 1991 it had been fashionable to predict a replay of the days when Britain, tsarist Russia and others battled for influence in the area.

"The implication, of course, is that the driving dynamic of the region, fuelled and lubricated by oil, will be the competition of great powers to the disadvantage of the people who live there," Talbott said.
"Our goal is to avoid, and actively to discourage, that atavistic outcome," he said in a speech at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.

The Caspian Sea basin is estimated to hold 100 billion to 200 billion barrels of oil worth up to $4 trillion. There has been intense rivalry over the routes of new pipelines to get the oil to the outside world.

Talbott, who has largely directed Washington's policy on Russia and other former Soviet states for the past four years, called for "the geopolitics of oil" to be conducted "in terms appropriate to the 21st century and not the 19th."

"Let's leave Rudyard Kipling and George McDonald Fraser where they belong -- on the shelves of historical fiction," he said in reference to the authors whose characters Kim and Flashman figured in the "Great Game."

Saying Washington wanted to see "all responsible players in the Caucasus and Central Asia be winners", Talbott said an essential first step was to resolve regional conflicts like those in Nagorno-Karabakh, Georgia and Tajikistan.
"Conflict resolution must be Job One for U.S. policy in the region: it is both the prerequisite for, and an accompaniment to, energy development," he said.

In recent months the United States, Russia and France and France have been promoting a drive to end the 9-year-old conflict over Nagorno-Karabakh, an enclave inside Azerbaijan which is inhabited mainly by Armenians.

Talbott said the effort was being hampered by a section of America's own Freedom Support Act of 1992 which was intended to help Armenia overcome an Azerbaijani blockade but had ended up limiting U.S. leverage with Baku.

Nevertheless, he said the U.S.-Russian-French initiative -- of which few details have been revealed -- had induced "some flexibility" among the parties to the conflict and hoped the end of the conflict was "not too far off."

A Republican senator charged on Monday that the administration's Central Asia policy was too "Russo-centric", and needed to be restructured to help the states in the region forge stronger ties among themselves and with the West.
"I believe we have lost valuable time because of this unbalanced approach," Sen. Sam Brownback of Kansas said in a speech to the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think-tank in Washington.

Brownback, who last week introduced an amendment to the Foreign Operations Appropriation Bill laying out his views, said he would soon be introducing legislation to provide an overall framework for policy towards the region.

Asked about Brownback's comments, Talbott said that while Russia had stirred up trouble among its neighbours in the past, he believed Russia was now working with the international community to resolve problems.

If Russia used the Commonwealth of Independent States, grouping most former Soviet republics, to curb its neighbours' independence, "the CIS will deserve to join that other set of initials, USSR, on the ash heap of history," he said.
